## Hands-on 2 – The menu {#hands-on-2-the-menu .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 4 in the browser lab is exploratory.** Try several specifications, read what each one does, and get a feel for which decisions move the estimate.

1. `try_spec()` with no arguments is the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR, and every argument defaults to it
2. Change **one decision** in `try_spec()` and read *b*, the claim-aligned partial *r*, the CR2 p and the placement among the `r fmt_n(nrow(spec_curve))`; then another. Three or four is plenty, and one option that is off the curve, to read why it is refused
3. `my_experiments()` lists every try side by side, the small multiverse that you have just built
4. Rerun the one that you would defend, so that it is your last try, and **submit it** with `submit_exploration()`; the cell prints a tag such as `amber-otter-42`, which marks your dot on the chart
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your dot appears on the class chart of the [Multiverse]({{< var live-results-url >}}) page within seconds, drawn as an **exploratory** result, and we read the dots of the whole class once everyone has submitted.
:::

::: notes
Now you work the menu, and this is exploration. Open Task 4 in the browser lab. The first cell calls `try_spec()` with no arguments, which is the reproduced specification, my own model, and every argument defaults to it. Change one decision and read what happens to the estimate, its CR2 p-value and its placement. Then another. Three or four tries is plenty, and ask for one option that is off the curve as well, and read the reason that comes back. `my_experiments()` lists the tries side by side. Then rerun whichever one you can argue for best, so that it is your last try, and submit it; the cell prints a tag that marks your dot on the class chart, labelled exploratory because you chose it after looking. I say it again: this is exploration, and it is the right way to learn the menu. [circulate; keep the Multiverse page on the screen]
:::
